Rijksmuseum. The Netherlands' national art museum, the Rijksmuseum was founded in 1798 and is housed in its iconic building from the eighteen-eighties, designed by Pierre Cuypers in the Gothic Revival style. The building was completed in 1885 as a symbol of Dutch national pride, and it remains a major monument with distinctive architectural features including a grand staircase and soaring halls. The museum preserves the world's finest collection of Dutch Golden Age painting and is the most visited museum in the Netherlands. Rembrandt's Night Watch is the centerpiece, a vast Baroque masterpiece that dominates the main gallery and encapsulates the painter's dramatic use of light and shadow and his psychological depth. Vermeer's The Milkmaid and Woman Reading a Letter exemplify the museum's strengths in Dutch domestic interiors and demonstrate Vermeer's luminous, understated technique. The comprehensive holdings of Golden Age painters also include Frans Hals, Jacob van Ruisdael, and Jan Steen, and these works document the seventeenth-century commercial and cultural flourishing of the Dutch Republic. Beyond painting, the museum holds Delftware ceramics, silverware, and decorative arts from the period, which contextualizes the museum within Dutch material culture as a whole. Between 2003 and 2013, the Rijksmuseum underwent a decade-long renovation with glass bridge additions designed by Cruz and Ortiz, modernizing its infrastructure while preserving its nineteenth-century character. These additions maintained the Night Watch's status as its iconic work and affirmed the museum's centrality to Amsterdam's cultural identity and tourism as the repository for understanding the Dutch Golden Age.
